transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-22 16:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood PM); Tom (CloudScale Eng Mgr), Jamal (CloudScale SRE), Rita (Product), Marta (Security)

Summary (auto): quick walkthrough of streaming timeout behaviors, queue saturation and graceful fallback patterns; proposed PoC and artifacts to run 2-week load test; discussed security and KMS concerns.

Topics (auto): streaming backpressure; queue/circuit breaker settings; long-context KV cache behavior; timeout/retry semantics; model fallbacks; monitoring + dashboards; PoC scope and next steps.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex: hey everybody, thanks for joining. we wanted to run through a focused demo today on streaming timeouts and what happens when queues saturate under sustained t p s loads - um, especially with long context sessions.
[00:17] Tom: yeah, that's our main worry — we saw timeouts last week when a batch job peaked and some of our chat sessions dropped.
[00:25] Priya: cool, i'll share my screen in a sec. quick callout: i'll demo both the hosted API path and the dedicated pool behaviour, highlight KV cache, and show fallback routing to smaller quantized variants. note: transcription may flip some product names.
[00:42] Jamal: when you say fallback routing, is that automatic or a policy we control? we can't have sticky routing that flips mid-session unless we can guarantee context continuity.
[00:55] Priya: good question. by default we route by policy - you can set latency-first or cost-first. when capacity gets constrained the router can opt for a compatible model variant (for example a 4bit-quantized MTok-13B) and the system will attempt to rehydrate KV cache. but rehydrate can add latency.
[01:13] Rita: rehydrate? like reloading the key value cache for the session? how long does that take?
[01:20] Priya: yeah, re-populating the KV cache can be expensive if the session is long — it depends on sequence length and the number of cached layers. typical rehydrate for a 10k token history might add 300-600ms in our numbers; in worst-case queue-saturated windows we saw up to 1.5s.
[01:36] Tom: 1.5s is a deal breaker for some flows. our SLA is 500ms p50 for interactive chat.
[01:44] Alex: understood, that's why we'll show circuit breaker patterns - degrade early and fall back to deterministic shorter-context responses or a downstream reranker.
[01:53] Priya: ok demo start. i'm hitting a synthetic load that simulates 5k concurrent sessions with 2k t p s sustained - long contexts 6k-12k tokens. watch the request queue window and the streaming client.
[02:10] [screen shares - console UI noise]
[02:25] Priya: you can see request queue depth spike — the runtime starts applying backpressure and we do a couple of things: (1) prioritize low-latency routes, (2) increase batching slightly to improve throughput, (3) apply early pixel-level truncation or summary prompts if configured.
[02:43] Jamal: what's 'early pixel-level truncation' — did you mean prefix truncation?
[02:48] Priya: sorry, yes prefix truncation. my mic dropped a syllable. the point is we can trim or summarize history server-side before synthesizing.
[02:56] Diego: also important: the streaming protocol uses chunked transfer/keep-alive; if the backend is overloaded we can return partial chunks and a header hint that indicates partial answer. clients should be resilient to partial frames.
[03:15] Tom: our client library is expecting SSE with a single final event, so partial frames break our rendering. can you force a finalizing frame even when overloaded?
[03:25] Priya: yes, Redwood supports a 'finalize-on-choke' flag that sends a compressed summary as final chunk then closes the stream. it's part of the streaming options in the SDK.
[03:36] Rita: how do we handle token accounting when we send summarized partials? cost concerns.
[03:42] Alex: accounting is per token processed; summaries still consume tokens but you can configure max-generation tokens to cap cost. we'll include that in the PoC pricing note.
[03:52] [05:00] Priya: moving to timeouts — there are two layers: client request timeout (eg 15s) and server-side generation timeout. when queue saturation occurs, the server may hit internal generation timeouts — we expose clear error codes: 429_queue_saturated, 524_generation_timeout, and a stream hint 207_incomplete_chunk.
[04:20] Jamal: do you recommend retries for 524 or should we do fallback to a smaller model?
[04:28] Priya: for 524 generation_timeout we recommend immediate fallback to a shorter-context or quantized variant instead of blind retries. retries can exacerbate saturation. we also suggest exponential backoff with jitter on 429s.
[04:40] Tom: is there a rate limiter at the customer layer we can control? we have bursty ETL that floods the endpoint.
[04:47] Alex: yes, you can set per-route quotas and token-limits and Redwood can return a 429 with a Retry-After header. For Dedicated customers we also surface a reserved concurrency pool and a modest burst bucket to smooth ETL spikes.
[05:00] [05:30] Priya: showing the console: here's a route config. notice the 'degradation policy' — we set thresholds for queue depth, then action: collapse-history or model-variant. you can also set a 'soft-ttl' to expire KV cache entries faster under memory pressure.
[05:55] Marta: from security side we need to know how cache is stored — is it encrypted, can we disable server KV cache?
[06:05] Priya: KV cache is encrypted at rest and in transit; for Private deployments you can bring your own KMS. we also provide an option to disable server-side KV cache and instead store a client-side compressed history blob if you need absolute control.
[06:20] Marta: ok good. please send the KMS integration docs.
[06:25] Alex: noted. i'll add that to the artifacts.
[06:30] [07:00] Priya: i'm toggling a synthetic failure mode now — simulating network jitter and short disconnects to the streaming client. you'll see retries and fallback in the logs.
[07:20] [console logs]
[07:30] Priya: the runtime surfaced 207_incomplete_chunk and then triggered finalize-on-choke. the client got a summarised final chunk. in the UI you can opt to surface heuristics: confidence, truncated_reason.
[07:45] Jamal: how accurate is the truncated_reason? we need to audit when summaries were served vs full text for downstream analytics.
[07:53] Priya: every truncated response emits an audit event with reason and session_id. we ship that to your observability : log sink or to the Redwood Console's event stream.
[08:05] Tom: if we need exact transcripts for audit purposes, can we persist full responses even if we serve a summary to the client?
[08:12] Priya: yes, you can configure 'persist_full_on_truncate' so backend persists the full generation to a secure store but sends a summarized stream to the user. that has storage and cost implications.
[08:25] Rita: for our use-case we want persisted full output for compliance but served summaries in UI. possible.
[08:30] Alex: ok moving on — monitoring. Priya, show the perf dashboard and SLO alerts.
[08:40] Priya: right. here's p50/p95/p99 latency by route, and a queue heatmap showing which worker pools were saturated. note the 'fallback event rate' panel — you can set alerts if fallback rate exceeds, say, 0.5% of requests in a day.
[09:00] Tom: can we export these metrics to our Prometheus?
[09:05] Priya: yes, we have exporters and a pushgateway integration; we also provide prebuilt Grafana dashboards.
[09:12] Jamal: what about tracing? we need end-to-end trace ids.
[09:16] Priya: Trace headers (x-request-id / traceparent) are preserved and surfaced. Redwood injects per-token timing annotations so you can see queue time vs kernel execution time.
[09:28] Tom: interesting — can we benchmark kernel time on our GPU types?
[09:33] Priya: for Private deployments yes; for Hosted we publish per-model performance profiles. we'll share the model perf spreadsheet.
[09:40] Alex: quick Q about client behavior: what should our frontend do on 429 vs 524 vs incomplete chunk?
[09:48] Priya: on 429: surface a soft throttle UI and retry after with exponential backoff; on 524: fall back to lighter model variant or shortened history; on 207_incomplete_chunk: show partial answer with an explicit tag 'incomplete' and queue a background request for a follow-up full generation if you need it.
[10:10] Rita: what about per-session sticky pins? again we cannot flip model mid-session without risking hallucination regressions.
[10:18] Priya: you can set sticky affinity for sessions. the router will only change variant if rehydrate is permitted and policy allows a small delta in model behavior — a canary ratio. many customers prefer to degrade history length instead of model class change.
[10:33] Tom: ok let's talk PoC scope and failure modes we want Redwood to exercise. we want three axes: latency-sensitive chat, long-context summarization, and batch ETL generation. test 5k sustained TPS for 48h and also run 30-min stress bursts to 12k TPS.
[10:50] Alex: good. we'll run those scenarios and capture queue depth, fallback rate, rehydrate latency, partial-chunk frequency, and server OOM events.
[11:00] Priya: log note: sometimes the transcription here will show 'K V cash' instead of KV cache; ignore that.
[11:05] Jamal: haha, yep seen that.
[11:10] Diego: on the Optimize side, we'll provide quantization recommendations and batching configs per workload; sometimes increasing batch size reduces per-token cost but raises p50 latency — that's the tradeoff you'll see.
[11:25] Tom: are there recommended defaults for chat vs summarization?
[11:28] Diego: chat: smaller batch sizes, lower max_generation_tokens, keep longer-kv ttl; summarization: larger batches, allow longer generation windows, consider offloading summary to a dedicated pool.
[11:40] Rita: one more security question: if we do persist_full_on_truncate, can we set retention policies?
[11:45] Priya: yes retention is configurable per-route. for Private you can use your own lifecycle policies; for Hosted we support configurable retention windows and auto-purge.
[11:55] Alex: ok wrapping up — recap and next steps.
[12:00] Alex: Recap: Redwood will run PoC with three workload profiles, share the backpressure runbook, provide KMS/SOC2 docs, and Priya will send load scripts. CloudScale will share traffic profile and prompts, and Marta will confirm compliance questions.
[12:15] Tom: thanks, we'll get those artifacts to you by Thursday.
[12:20] Marta: thanks, appreciate the finalize-on-choke option. please include an audit trail example in the security docs.
[12:27] Alex: will do. thanks everyone.

End of call
